title: Slicing, Copying, and Tuples
objective: Extract part of a list with slicing, tell apart a real copy of a list from an alias to the same list, and store fixed values in a tuple.

sourceAlignment.title: Python Crash Course, 3rd Edition
sourceAlignment.author: Eric Matthes
sourceAlignment.note: Alignment metadata only. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: A slice pulls out part of a list without changing the original. party[1:3] returns a new list containing the items at index 1 up to, but not including, index 3. Leaving off either number means "to the start" or "to the end": party[:2] takes the first two items, party[2:] takes everything from index 2 onward. A slice is a real list of its own, so you can loop over it just like any other list.

Writing new_list = old_list does not make a copy — it makes new_list point at the exact same list as old_list. Change one and the other changes too, because there's really only one list with two names. To get an independent copy, slice the whole thing with old_list[:], which builds a brand-new list containing the same items.

A tuple is a list-like sequence that cannot be changed after it's created. You write one with parentheses (or nothing at all) and commas, like coords = (10, 20). Tuples are useful for values that should stay fixed, such as coordinates or a screen size — trying to reassign coords[0] raises a TypeError.
explanation.rule: A slice like list_name[a:b] copies a range into a new list; list_name[:] copies the whole thing; plain assignment (new_list = old_list) only creates another name for the same list; tuples are written with parentheses and can never be changed.

examples.title: Slicing a Party
examples.code:
party = ["Nyx", "Bram", "Odele", "Fen"]
front_two = party[:2]
print(front_two)
for member in party[1:3]:
    print(member)
examples.note: party[:2] takes the first two items; party[1:3] takes index 1 and 2, stopping before index 3.

examples.title: Alias vs. Copy
examples.code:
original = [1, 2, 3]
alias = original
copy = original[:]
alias.append(4)
print(original)
print(copy)
examples.note: alias points at the same list as original, so appending to alias changes original too. copy is independent, so it stays [1, 2, 3].

checks.question: Given items = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50], what does items[1:3] return?

feedback.correct: Correct — index 1 up to, but not including, index 3 is [20, 30].
feedback.incorrect: The slice includes the start index but stops just before the end index.

checks.question: If b = a (no slicing) and then b.append(9), what happens to a?
options: Nothing — a and b are separate lists
a also gains the new item, since a and b are the same list

feedback.correct: Correct — without slicing, b is just another name for a's list.
feedback.incorrect: Plain assignment doesn't copy a list — it makes a second name for the same one.

assignment.title: Scout Party
assignment.brief: Write scouting_report(party) that slices out the scouts, walks the front line with a for loop over a slice, demonstrates the alias-vs-copy difference, and prints a fixed pair of coordinates as a tuple.
requirements: Slice party[1:3] into a variable called scouts and print it labeled "Scouts:".
Loop over party[:2] with a for loop, printing "Front line: {name}" for each.
Create same_list = party (an alias) and copy_list = party[:] (a real copy).
Append "Kestrel" to same_list, then print party labeled "Party now:" and copy_list labeled "Copy unaffected:".
Create a tuple coords = (10, 20) and print it labeled "Coordinates:".

scouting_report(["Nyx", "Bram", "Odele", "Fen"])
assignment.solutionCode:
def scouting_report(party):
    scouts = party[1:3]
    print("Scouts:", scouts)
    for member in party[:2]:
        print(f"Front line: {member}")
    same_list = party
    copy_list = party[:]
    same_list.append("Kestrel")
    print("Party now:", party)
    print("Copy unaffected:", copy_list)
    coords = (10, 20)
    print("Coordinates:", coords)

scouting_report(["Nyx", "Bram", "Odele", "Fen"])

assignment.outputCheckLabel: scouting_report([...]) prints the slice, front line, alias/copy comparison, and tuple

hints: party[1:3] grabs index 1 and 2 — two items, stopping before index 3.
party[:2] is its own list, so you can put it directly after 'in' in a for loop.
same_list = party does not copy anything; party[:] is what actually builds a new, independent list.
Because same_list and party are the same list, appending to same_list changes what party prints too — but copy_list was built before that append, so it stays as it was.
A tuple just needs parentheses and a comma: (10, 20).
